Flint|United States of America.f: General Motors was founded in Flint in 1908, and carriage-making earned the city the nickname Vehicle City.

Clarksburg|United States of America.f: Randolph Academy, founded here in 1787, was the first such school west of the Allegheny Mountains.

Yakutat|United States of America.f: The Yakutat borough is about six times the size of Rhode Island but had only 657 residents in 2020.

Wausau|United States of America.f: The name Wausau comes from the Ojibwe word waasa, meaning a faraway place.

Fayetteville (NC)|United States of Ameri.f: Fayetteville was the first US city named in honor of the Marquis de Lafayette, who visited in 1825.

Pasco|United States of America.f: Pasco was named by a railroad engineer after Cerro de Pasco, a city in the Peruvian Andes where he had built a railroad.

Minot|United States of America.f: A tent town sprang up overnight in 1886 and passed 5,000 people within five months, earning Minot the nickname Magic City.

Prescott|United States of America.f: Prescott's rodeo, running continuously since 1888, calls itself the World's Oldest Rodeo.

Yakima|United States of America.f: When the railroad bypassed the town in 1884, over 100 buildings were moved on rollers by horse teams to the new depot site.

Allentown|United States of America.f: The Liberty Bell was hidden in Allentown from September 1777 to June 1778 to keep it from the British army.

Sun Valley|United States of America.f: Sun Valley was the first destination winter resort in the US, built by the Union Pacific's Averell Harriman to boost train ridership.

Kodiak|United States of America.f: Settled by Russians in 1792 as Paul's Harbor, Kodiak was the capital of Russian Alaska.

Corpus Christi|United States of America.f: Spanish explorer Pineda is credited with naming the bay in 1519 after the Feast of Corpus Christi, the day he was thought to arrive.

Las Cruces|United States of America.f: The Battle of El Bracito, an early clash of the Mexican-American War, was fought near Las Cruces on Christmas Day 1846.

Gainesville|United States of America.f: The sports drink Gatorade was invented in Gainesville in the 1960s to refresh the University of Florida football team.

Monroe|United States of America.f: Joseph Biedenharn, the first Coca-Cola bottler, moved to Monroe in 1913, and he and his son helped found Delta Air Lines.

Williston|United States of America.f: The huge Williston Basin, rich in oil, coal and potash, is named after this city.

Wilkes-Barre|United States of America.f: Wilkes-Barre was named for John Wilkes and Isaac Barre, two British members of Parliament who supported colonial America.

Gillette|United States of America.f: The town began as Donkey Town, named for Donkey Creek, before the railroad renamed it for surveyor Edward Gillette.

Baton Rouge|United States of America.f: Baton Rouge has been ruled by six different nations, including France, Spain, Britain and the Confederacy.

Saint Cloud|United States of America.f: St. Cloud is named after a suburb of Paris, which was itself named for the 6th-century monk Clodoald.

Cordova|United States of America.f: No road links Cordova to any other Alaskan community except Eyak, so a plane or ferry is required to get there.

Ketchikan|United States of America.f: Ketchikan's ZIP code 99950 is the highest-numbered ZIP code in the United States.

Bishop|United States of America.f: Bishop calls itself the Mule Capital of the World and has held a week-long Mule Days festival since 1969.

Presque Isle|United States of America.f: Originally called Fairbanks, the town took the French word for peninsula, as the Aroostook River and a stream form one.

Columbia (MO)|United States of America.f: Columbia's Christian Female College was the first college for women west of the Mississippi River.

Stillwater|United States of America.f: Stillwater was part of the first Oklahoma Land Run in 1889 and is home to the National Wrestling Hall of Fame and Museum.

Chattanooga|United States of America.f: In 2010 Chattanooga launched the first government-provided one-gigabit-per-second Internet service in the United States.

International Falls|United States of Ame.f: Nicknamed the Icebox of the Nation, it averages 109.4 days a year with a high below freezing.

Manhattan|United States of America.f: Founded by New England settlers as a Free-State town, Manhattan is nicknamed the Little Apple after New York's Big Apple.

Brownsville|United States of America.f: Brownsville saw the first engagements of the Mexican-American War, at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma.

Moab|United States of America.f: Residents named the town Moab in 1880, and an 1890 petition to rename it Vina failed.

Grand Forks|United States of America.f: Canadian fur traders called the spot Les Grandes Fourches for the fork where the Red River and Red Lake River meet.

Vero Beach|United States of America.f: A mastodon or mammoth carved on a bone found near Vero Beach was examined and probably made in the Pleistocene.

Gallup|United States of America.f: Named for a railroad paymaster, Gallup was a popular location for Hollywood Westerns in the 1940s and 1950s.

Binghamton|United States of America.f: The flight simulator was invented in Binghamton, and IBM was founded nearby.

Dickinson|United States of America.f: Dickinson is home to the Ukrainian Cultural Institute, which runs a museum for the local Ukrainian community.

Garden City|United States of America.f: Locals refused to cut Main Street's trees for the first telephone line, so the poles were set down the center of the street.

Wilmington (DE)|United States of America.f: Wilmington sits on the site of Fort Christina, the first Swedish settlement in North America, founded in 1638.

Parkersburg|United States of America.f: A major oil refining center in the late 1800s, Parkersburg's Camden refinery company was sold to Standard Oil in 1875.
